The powder for the laser cladding welding process of alloy CoWAlloy2Mod was manufactured by Nanoval GmbH & Co. KG (Berlin/Germany) by gas atomization and subsequent sieving.
Cubes with edge lengths of 10 mm were welded on a plate of Ni-base superalloy Alloy247, using a micro cladding welding process at Siemens AG (Berlin/Germany).
All three materials were heat treated in a 3-step heating process at 1230 °C for 2 h, 1080 °C for 2 h, and 870 °C for 20 h.
PWA795 was arc-melted from welding wires (Polymet, West Chester Township/USA) and CoWAlloy2 was manufactured, cast and hot-rolled at Vacuumschmelze GmbH & Co. KG (Hanau/Germany).
PWA795 was arc-melted from welding wires (Polymet, West Chester Township/USA) and CoWAlloy2 was manufactured, cast and hot-rolled at Vacuumschmelze GmbH & Co. KG (Hanau/Germany).

The reference materials PWA795 and CoWAlloy2 were cast instead of welded as the cast specimen were already available and there were no suitable powders present for these materials.

The γ’ volume fraction of the secondary γ’ precipitates for CoWAlloy2Mod was determined as 42 ± 1%. The slightly higher γ’ volume fraction of CoWAlloy2 compared to CoWAlloy2Mod can be explained by a higher content of the γ’ forming elements W and Ni in CoWAlloy2 and the higher concentration of Cr in CoWAlloy2Mod, which reduces the γ’ fraction in Co-base superalloys.
This yields a calculated γ’ volume fraction f γ’ of 47.5%.

The porosity in CoWAlloy2Mod is about 1.7% but there are only a few larger pores and no cracks present. Due to their spherical size and shape, the pores are mainly gas pores generated during the powder manufacturing or welding process.
The layer architecture of the as-welded condition of CoWAlloy2Mod, induced by the layer-wise building process, can be seen in Figure 2a with an average layer height of about 150 μm.
CoWAlloy2 and CoWAlloy2Mod exhibit a similar strength over the complete strain and strain rate range, which is by a factor of around two higher compared to PWA795.

In agreement with the SRS compression tests, the creep curves of the three investigated alloys at 950 °C and 100 MPa (Figure 4b) reveal that PWA795 has the lowest creep strength.
Different from the SRJ tests CoWAlloy2 exhibits a higher creep strength than CoWAlloy2Mod.
